title: THE REST IN THE SONG THAT TAKES A MILLION YEARS
deck: A farming world's sun has gone three percent grey, and what is dimming it takes a million years to finish a phrase. Illuminara has one night with it, a governor who owes forty thousand people a harvest, and a rule that she will not speak for either side.
shape: Seven scenes across a night, a test and a silence: a sun that is only slightly wrong, a night spent keeping time with a cold slow mind and testing her first answer until it could fail, a table where a governor, an astronomer and a ship's doctor each hold the part of the risk that is theirs, a three-day pause whose number could have embarrassed her and the vote that follows it, a school that chooses a single note and a rule that lets the colony take it back, one night in the silence when the colony must decide with a life on the line, and the afternoon the sky answers by a hair and a gap is left open in the network's band.

scenes.title: A Few Percent
paragraphs: *Kestrel, Terrace Nine, the colony house · day one, noon*

The sun over Kestrel had been losing light for twenty-two months, and nobody who looked at it could have said so. It rose at its proper hour and stood at its proper height, and the barley on the terraces leaned toward it, a little thin, a little late, three weeks from a harvest that would not fill the granaries.

Illuminara stood in the doorway of the colony house with the noon on her face and a sheet of photometer readings in her hand, and understood why the colony had taken so long to be afraid. Three point two percent was less than a passing cloud. It was only that this cloud had not passed.

Governor Ilse Maran had the terrace charts spread on a trestle table, weighted with seed jars. She was a square grey woman in work boots, and she did not offer Illuminara a chair, which Illuminara took as a courtesy. It meant she was not going to be managed.

**Ilse Maran**  
Barley sets at ninety-seven percent of full light or it does not set. We are at ninety-six point eight. If this harvest fails we eat the seed reserve, and if the spring one fails we ask Tern for bread, and Tern has terraces of its own.

**Hedda Rask**  
It began twenty-two months ago, when we tripled the beacons' output for a new shipping lane. That is the part I cannot make into an accident.

Hedda Rask ran the beacon office and talked about the sky the way other people talk about a debt. The Hollin had been in the catalogue as a sky-sound for longer than Kestrel's beacons had pinged the dark: cold gas strung along a whole arm of the galaxy, singing one phrase that took, by her reckoning, a million years from first note to last.

**Illuminara**  
A dust lane drifting across your sightline would do the same.

**Hedda Rask**  
It would. And dust reddens. It takes the blue first. Ours takes the same share of every colour.

**Illuminara**  
You put that in your report.

**Hedda Rask**  
In the second paragraph. The Governor stopped believing it at the second paragraph.

**Ilse Maran**  
A cloud that dims us evenly because we spoke to it. I have a farm, not a faith. What I have is a plan: ten times the beacon power, in the Hollin's own cadence, which Hedda has decoded for six years. An apology and a request. We are sorry. Please stop.

**Hedda Rask**  
I am not certain it is an apology in their grammar. I am not certain it is not a shout.

**Ilse Maran**  
Then tell me what is certain, because I have forty thousand people here, twelve thousand on Tern, and a hospital ship, the Linden Reach, with every transfer routed on those beacons. I will not hear that the answer is to switch off the sky.

Illuminara looked at the terraces through the open door. She could do the thing the Governor had not quite asked. A body of cold gas, a few light-hours deep, was lying across a sun, and she could clear it before dark, the way a person clears a table with her arm.

**Ilse Maran**  
You could, couldn't you. Burn it off.

**Illuminara**  
By tonight. It is a body, Governor, and it is in the middle of a sentence. I would be stopping a note that began before there were people to hear it, and I would not know what I had stopped. I will not do it. I want to find out what the damping is saying first. My window can hold one node of the Hollin in the same light as me for a night. I won't speak for you, and I won't promise anything in Kestrel's name.

**Ilse Maran**  
You will learn. You will promise nothing. And if you come back with a poem?

**Illuminara**  
Then I will tell you it is a poem.
Maran folded her arms. It was not agreement. It was a woman who had run out of better offers.

scenes.title: One Breath
paragraphs: *The seed barn, Terrace Nine, a window raised in the dark · night one, 21:00*

She raised the window at the far end of the barn, from the one rule she trusted most, that two minds who could not share a world could still stand in one light without either being rewritten by it. The barn smelled of dust and seed husks. At the other end of the floor, so slowly that for the first hour she took it for stillness, a band of cold pale light began to breathe.

It was not a face and it was not a voice. It was a long grey-silver swell along the wall, rising, holding, falling, and each swell took the whole of the night. The window could not make her quick enough to follow a million years, or the node quick enough to follow her. It could only fix an exchange: one night of hers against the smallest thing the node could mean, a single breath that took nine days outside the barn. She would get one breath of it, and it would get one breath of her.

She tried Rask's decoded cadence first, wanting to be wrong about it before she was wrong in front of Maran. She shaped her voice to the Hollin cadence, an apology and a request, and slowed it to the length of the swell. The band narrowed. The grey thickened until the light behind it was a thread, and the swell, which had been generous, drew itself in like a hand closing. She stopped. She knew only that it had made itself smaller, and that this was not what a guest should do to a host.

*That is what ten times the power would have been,* she thought, *in a voice it could not turn away from.* She sat down on a seed sack and let the window go quiet. The light eased. It did not widen. It stayed small for a long while, the way a person stays small after a loud voice has left the room.

For the rest of the hour she learned the swell: rise, hold, a long shallow shoulder, and then, a third of the way through the night, a flat pale floor. A rest, as plainly in the shape of the thing as a rest is in a bar of music. Over the floor, like frost on a window, lay the grey damping, thickest exactly there.

The frost was what she noticed first, and she distrusted it, because thick frost over a quiet place could mean a dozen things. So she counted what else lay in the grey: the ghosts of earlier floors, laid down and scraped away. Seventy-four. Twenty-two months was about six hundred and seventy days, and six hundred and seventy divided by nine was seventy-four and a little. A rest attempted once in every breath since the beacons tripled, and scraped every time.

The window carried the colony's beacons to her as the node heard them: one unbroken scratch across the place where the rest should have been quiet. It had no word for stop. It could only do what a patient being does when made to sing over a noise, and lean on the noise until it was soft.
*The leaning is the veil. It is trying to hear its rest.*

That was a pattern, and a pattern is a way of being wrong. If the node were merely oppressed by light, any dark would ease it, so she took the window dark for a minute in the hold, where the band was loud and easy. Nothing changed. The frost lay where it was. Had it eased there, she would have gone back to Maran with nothing but dust.

She waited for the floor. When it came round she took the window dark again, no lamp, no voice, nothing of hers that could be mistaken for a pulse, and held it. It was the longest silence she had kept in her life, harder than any hold of a sun or a door, because the thing she wanted most was to speak.

The frost began to draw back from the floor in the first part of her dark. Then the floor opened, wide and level, and for a little while she stood in a room made entirely of quiet that had been made for her.
There was a small bright ripple at the end of it, where the band lifted again, fast, the fastest thing she had seen it do. A downbeat. She counted it against the dark.

She had one note left in her, and she asked first, in the only way she had. She sat at the edge of the lifted band and hummed one low tone, quieter than breath, and held it as long as she could stand to. The node did not narrow. It did not deepen. At the edge of her tone the band widened by the width of a hair, and held.

It was not a yes. It was a margin. She sat in it until the grey of the barn windows came up behind her, and in the last minutes of the night she understood something that surprised her by its tenderness. For the whole of the node's one breath, she had been the shortest thing it had ever met. A grace note. She had been called a great many things in her life, and she had never been a breath, and she was sorry, a little, when the window let her go.

scenes.title: What a Governor Owes
paragraphs: *The colony house, the long table · day two, 07:00*

Dr. Amadou Ferre had come down from the Linden Reach on the dawn shuttle, still in his ship's grey. He was a lean man with a physician's patience and none of it for sky-sounds. Maran had given the fourth chair to the one person present who held six hundred beds.

**Ilse Maran**  
Say it in one sentence I can put to a vote.

**Illuminara**  
Their breath is nine days. Three for the frost to thin, then six of rest, ending in a downbeat. I was shown it folded into one night. Our beacons are a scratch across the rest, so it has been scraping the floor for twenty-two months, and the veil is how it does that. I got it wrong once before I got it less wrong. I said Hedda's apology to it. It closed up. A louder one would close it harder.
Rask had gone very still. Her apology had been six years of her working life.

**Hedda Rask**  
I would rather know.

**Illuminara**  
I am sorry. It was the only way to learn it, and it cost a node an hour.

**Amadou Ferre**  
A night with a cloud is not evidence. It is an experience. I have thirty transfers a day on those beacons and my patients are not a sample.

**Illuminara**  
No. They are not. I am not asking you to turn anything off on my word. I am asking Hedda for the cheapest test that could prove me wrong.
Rask already had a pencil. She wrote on the back of a terrace chart: the channels that carried nothing a person could die of missing, a third of the beacon power, three days.

**Hedda Rask**  
Two things could be true, and they keep different clocks. If this is only load, the veil eases the hour we cut, in proportion. If it is a node clearing a floor, the frost has to thin first. Nothing for fifty or sixty hours, then it lifts. A third of the power should buy a third of a third of the three point two: point three six, give or take a tenth, grey, not red. If it moves in the first day I will write that it was load. If I see a full one percent, or nothing at all, I will write that it was dust, in the first paragraph.

**Amadou Ferre**  
Then Tern has spoken. The clinic director wrote this last night and made me promise to read it to your table.
He unfolded a sheet.

**Amadou Ferre**  
Three days' delay on the insulin we can bear. We have nine days on the shelf. If a child comes early we will say so, and you will lift it. She has signed it. I would have preferred her to say no. She did not.

**Ilse Maran**  
Now hear mine. The silence is not mine to order and it is not hers. The assembly votes. Whoever says no keeps their light on, and I will not send a warden to put it out. And the stop clause is mine. If a link fails and someone is dying for it, I lift the silence on that link by my own hand, and I say so before it starts, so nobody learns it afterward.

**Illuminara**  
That is a better design than the one I brought. I will not touch the clause.

**Ilse Maran**  
I know. That is why I am keeping it.

**Amadou Ferre**  
One thing more. If the band is the trouble, cut a notch around it. Why does anyone go dark for nine days?

**Hedda Rask**  
Around what? We have never heard its note. It has been under frost for twenty-two months. A notch cut blind is one more scratch, and retuning eleven hundred beacons is a season's work on a guess. The silence buys the thing we do not have, which is where it keeps its note.
Maran stood, and for the first time looked at Illuminara as one looks at a guest who has stayed, not at a tool that has come.

**Ilse Maran**  
You could have burned it off. I asked you to, in front of my people. Why did you not?

**Illuminara**  
Because it was singing. I did not know what, and then I did. I would rather lose a day with you than be the one who finished its sentence.

scenes.title: Three Days
paragraphs: *The beacon office, Terrace Nine · day three, 06:00, the pause begins*

The assembly voted the small test through in an afternoon: a third of the power, the channels that carried nothing a person could die of missing, three days. At six in the morning Rask's keepers brought them down one by one, and the silence went through the colony like a change in air pressure. Nothing happened. Nothing was meant to, not yet.

Illuminara waited in the office because Rask asked her to, and because she had learned in the barn that waiting could be work. The photometer plot did nothing on the first day, and nothing on the second, and Rask walked the length of the room nine times without speaking.

Late on the second night, at hour fifty-eight by the log, the line began to lift, slowly and smoothly and without any shape that dust would have made. Rask put her hand flat on the desk beside the screen, as if the desk were a table at which a hard word was about to be said. At the end of the third day she read the number aloud.

**Hedda Rask**  
Point two eight.

**Illuminara**  
Inside your band.

**Hedda Rask**  
Inside my band, at the low edge of it, and grey, colour by colour the same. I hate it, a little. I had a very good explanation about dust.

On the fourth morning the beacons came back and the dent healed behind them like a thumbprint in dough. The ship's narrow laser links had stayed up throughout, carrying the hospital traffic on a beam too thin to touch the band, and the veil had not so much as flinched at them.
The assembly met again that midnight, on the larger question, and Illuminara sat at the back with her hands in her lap because the question was not hers. Maran put it to Rask in front of everyone.

**Ilse Maran**  
Say what the test showed. And say what it did not.

**Hedda Rask**  
It showed this is not load. Load would have eased in the first hours, in proportion, and this waited fifty-eight hours and then lifted. Something is clearing its floor. It did not show the floor. A third of the power for three days only reached the frost, and the floor is six days long, and nothing short of the full silence lets it begin. Nine days is the smallest dark that gets one whole rest to its end. Less and we have thinned the frost and gone home.

The vote was sixty-one percent. Not the whole of it, and Maran did not pretend otherwise. She read the result aloud and the dissent beside it, and the name of Dov Karlsen in the dissent. He was already standing, a big man in a canvas coat holding his hat.

**Dov Karlsen**  
The ford on the hill road floods in a night and cannot be seen from the road. My lamp is the only thing between a hauler's cart and four feet of water. I will put it out the day you put another light on that ford. Not before.

**Hedda Rask**  
It is a plain lamp, Dov. There is no ping in it. I measured it, and it is nothing in the band.

**Dov Karlsen**  
Then you have no quarrel with it.

**Ilse Maran**  
I have none. It burns. What it costs this assembly is mine to carry, and I will send no warden.
He sat down without thanking her. Nobody in the hall thought he should have.

scenes.title: Nine Days
paragraphs: *Kestrel, the school hall · the silence, day two*

It was an odd quiet. The colony had never before heard its own sky. Wind through the barley carried as far as the school hall, and on the second morning someone laughed out loud at nothing and then stopped, startled.

Maran had put a question to the school, not Illuminara: if a voice was to enter at the end of the rest, whose would it be, and what would it say? The Hollin were a sky, she said, and the school was the part of Kestrel the sky would outlive.
Ilyan Voss was ten and had brought a list. He stood on a chair in the hall to read it.

**Ilyan Voss**  
It cannot be a word, because the Hollin do not have our words and Hedda says an apology made them close up. It has to be a note. One note. We vote on how high. And we write down what makes us stop. If it narrows when we sing, the dish goes quiet that month, and we chalk it on the dish so nobody can pretend they did not know.

**Illuminara**  
You are choosing the interval above their held band. A fifth, a sixth, a second. The Hollin have no reason to take any of them.

**Ilyan Voss**  
It made room. You said room. Room is for a person.
Illuminara had been asked in the corridor and twice in the yard which interval it should be, and had refused each time. She would not be the voice the colony hid behind later.

**Illuminara**  
I won't pick it. I could, and you would believe me, and it would be mine, not Kestrel's.

**Ilyan Voss**  
Then I pick the sixth. It is the first two notes of the harvest song. Everyone knows it. If it is the wrong one, it is still ours.

A girl in the back row said the fifth, because it was simpler and could not be mistaken for anything else, and she was right that it was simpler. They voted by hands, then by counting. A hundred and twelve for the sixth, ninety-seven for the fifth. Nobody cried. Ilyan went red to the ears and sat down hard.

scenes.title: The Ship Link
paragraphs: *The beacon office · the silence, day six, 03:00*

On the sixth night the laser relay on the ridge failed, and the ship's link fell back on the one road left to it, the broadcast carrier, which was a beacon like any other. On Tern a woman was in premature labour. The one specialist who could guide the surgical team by voice was on Kestrel. Maran came into the office without knocking, Ferre behind her with his coat open over his nightshirt.

**Ilse Maran**  
I am lifting the silence on the ship link. Only the ship link. I said I would say so first, and I am saying it.

**Hedda Rask**  
That carrier is in the band, Ilse. It is a scratch across the floor. I have not tested this. I could not.

**Ilse Maran**  
Then it costs what it costs. Open it.

Illuminara said nothing. The decision was not hers, and she did not insult it by agreeing. She watched Rask turn the dial, and watched the photometer line, which had been lifting for three days, stop and tremble.
The specialist spoke into the link for forty minutes. The child was born at six past four and was well. When the carrier went quiet again, Rask sat a long moment with her pencil above the log.

**Hedda Rask**  
It lost the floor. It did not scrape it, it lost it, and it is looking for it again. I said nine days and I wrote it on a chart. I am wrong by about ten hours, and I will be wrong by more if anyone coughs.

**Ilse Maran**  
Then the silence holds ten hours past the ninth. The ship link stays open for any life that needs it, and we say so now, in this room, not later. Hedda, write it.

**Amadou Ferre**  
And Tern waits one more night.

**Ilse Maran**  
Tern waits one more night. Tell the director.

Ferre flew the ship's courier, the Wren, on the seventh day with a crate of cold-chain insulin and a surgeon. Rask's keepers drew idle wages from the common store with embarrassment, and stood on their dark roofs in the evenings looking across at Dov Karlsen's amber lamp on the hill, and said nothing, in the way neighbours say nothing.

By the ninth day the veil had thinned to a long even grey over every colour, the light of Kestrel's sun coming slowly home, and the node, which had never in twenty-two months been allowed a whole rest, was being allowed this one.

scenes.title: A Gap the Width of a Sixth
paragraphs: *Kestrel, the school roof · the tenth day, 16:10*

The downbeat came ten hours late, the small bright ripple Illuminara had counted in the dark barn. Rask watched it rise in the trace like a fish rising and stood back. Then the trace did something she had not logged in six years: three short pulses at the old ping interval, an echo of the last ping the beacons had sent before the silence, and then not again.

**Hedda Rask**  
It gave our ping back once, at its own speed, and it will not do it twice. Nobody asked it to. I do not know what that means. I will write that it did it, and that no one asked.
Illuminara knew a margin when she saw one.

**Hedda Rask**  
That is the end of the rest, and now I can hear where it keeps its note, which I could not before. The beacons come back with a notch cut around it. The dish sings in the notch. It is yours.

The school's old transmitter was a rusted dish the children had been allowed to oil and aim. On its rim, in chalk, in a boy's blocky hand, was the rule: if the band narrows, we stop. Maran held the switch. She did not make a speech. Ilyan stood a little to the side of his own idea, and the note went out, a single tone, a sixth above the held band, low and clear and steady.
Illuminara stood on the school roof and watched a boy listen to the sky, and did not say what the node would make of it, because she did not know.

The barley came in twenty-six days later, a tenth thinner than a founding year and a week late, and the lower terraces never fully recovered. Maran tapped the seed reserve she had sworn not to touch, and said so aloud at the granary door.

**Hedda Rask**  
The note has gone out once more since, on the first. It has not narrowed and it has not widened. It has not answered again either. I think they held a place and it was taken, or I think they let it be taken. The log gets only that.
Ilyan Voss stood on the terrace wall in his school coat, shading his eyes. He looked up at the sun, which was only the sun, white and unreasonable and warm.

**Ilyan Voss**  
Is it ours?

**Illuminara**  
It is in the same song as the rest, and it is one note in a million years. I don't know what it heard.

**Ilyan Voss**  
It is still ours. I wiped the chalk on the first and wrote it again.

Illuminara walked out between the barley rows with the noon on her face. It was warmer than on the day she arrived, by an amount three percent could not have named. Behind her, from the beacon office, the eleven hundred beacons went on pinging the dark in their band, all but one place in it. The school dish sang there on the first of every month, one tone, and the gap in the network was exactly the width of a boy's sixth.

critic_line: Illuminara declines to burn a nameless cold mind off Kestrel's sun, learns by testing her own first answer that an apology closes it and a held silence lets it keep its note, and helps the colony turn a three-day pause into a nine-day silence with a stop clause, a dissenter's lamp and a school's chalked rule, so the sun clears, the node finishes its first whole rest in twenty-two months and the network keeps a notch where it sings.
